$FIGR This is a major strategic win for Figure, as $BAC becomes partnered with Figure as a DART participant, potentially removing a major obstacle for originators and investors who want to use Figure while maintaining their existing warehouse financing relationships with BofA.  DART is Figure's blockchain-based alternative to MERS, the traditional mortgage registry. It tracks loan ownership and interests, enabling automated updates as loans change hands. The underlying infrastructure has applications across additional loan types, and Figure's 10-K document noted that DART adoption was 87% across Figure ecosystem loans (from just 2% in 2024).  What's most interesting to me is what this could signify for Figure's future. Adding one of America's largest banks validates the infrastructure and advantages of DART vs MERS, likely accelerates institutional adoption, and opens the door to greater financing activity on Figure Connect.   This agreement also underscores what has become a reality: Figure is a platform, with 72% of their income derived from the ecosystem and platform, not their own loans. DART is just one of many parts of their technology flywheel which is accelerating into 2027's, "Year of the Upsell."  @MBTannenbaum's "More to come for this partnership," is particularly intriguing.

Flying somewhere for Thanksgiving? How you should use sunlight depends on how long you're staying. ⠀ 3 days or less: stay on home time ⠀ • Your body clock can only shift a couple of hours a day, even if you do everything right ⠀ • On a short trip, by the time you've adjusted, you're flying home and doing it all over again ⠀ • So stay on your home schedule as much as you can. Get your sunlight at the time you'd normally wake up back home, and keep the room dark when you'd normally be asleep ⠀ More than 3 days: shift to local time ⠀ If you flew east (like LA to New York) ⠀ • This is the harder direction, because your body has to fall asleep earlier than it wants to ⠀ • Get bright sunlight in the morning at your destination to pull your clock earlier ⠀ • Keep evenings dim so you can wind down sooner ⠀ If you flew west (like New York to LA) ⠀ • This is the easier direction, because staying up a little later comes naturally ⠀ • Get sunlight in the late afternoon and early evening to help push your clock later ⠀ Either way ⠀ • Don't try to fix everything in one day. Shifting about 1 to 3 hours a day is realistic ⠀ • Sunlight is your best tool for any of this, so get outside as soon as you land

How to validate an idea using Reddit:  1. Search the Problem  Go to Reddit and search for the pain point (e.g., "hate managing invoices" or "can't find good freelance designers") your idea solves.  And set the filter to Top / All Time.  2. Read the Posts Like a Heatmap  If you see dozens of threads complaining about the same problem across multiple subreddits, that's a real problem.  Then, we all realize there is no solution or only a partial one.  3. Check the Upvotes / Comments  High upvotes + many comments = strong pain, active community, real demand.  Low engagement = niche problem or weak urgency, people don't care enough  4. "Someone Should Build This" Signal  Search phrases like "I wish there was an app", "why doesn't X exist", or "I'd pay for...", these are goldmines.  Users are literally handing you validated ideas.  5. Spot the Workarounds  If people are sharing DIY solutions (spreadsheets, manual processes, duct-tape tools), that's a strong signal.  This means the problem is real and no good solution exists yet.  6. Find Targeted Subreddit  Check which subreddit the complaints live in.  That community = your first customer base. You can post there, run surveys, or do direct outreach.

Google’s commercial TPU business is shifting from internal infrastructure into an aggressive third-party merchant operation. With Google’s 2026 capital expenditure projected around $195B–$205B, selling custom silicon shifts severe data centre build-out costs directly to buyers, with Barclays forecasting third-party TPU revenue could hit $252.7B by 2028.  The commercial rollout is already anchored by major players. Broadcom filings show Anthropic plans 1GW of Ironwood in 2026, scaling to 5GW of TPU v8i in 2027 and 10GW in 2028, while Meta signed multi-billion-dollar deals and the BlackRock JV targets 0.5GW by 2027. Google is positioning TPUs as the primary market alternative to Nvidia.  Hardware clustering gives Google a defined timing window. The TPU v8T supercluster links 9,600 chips via optical circuit switches sharing 2PB of HBM memory, compared to Nvidia’s current 72-GPU NVL72 limit. If Nvidia’s higher-density architectures face manufacturing delays into 2028, Google’s 2027 TPU capacity of 8.8M–10M units directly challenges market supply.  The financial trade-off lies in structural margin dilution. Google Cloud’s operating margin expanded to 35.6% on $24.8B in revenue, but Morgan Stanley estimates merchant TPU margins at just ~30% due to pass-through costs on networking, liquid cooling, and power delivery. As hardware systems outgrow pure cloud rentals, overall business margins face clear downward pressure.  Converting these projected order books into realised cash hinges on two supply-chain bottlenecks: HBM allocations and customer balance sheets. Google and Nvidia are set to absorb roughly 75% of global HBM output through 2027, requiring heavy upfront vendor cash commitments while Anthropic relies on ongoing debt and equity financing to absorb multi-gigawatt hardware deliveries.

$META's Muse download numbers measure Meta's distribution, which was never in doubt. What decides whether Muse is a business is what the agent completes for a user, and nothing reported this week measures that.  Sensor Tower puts Muse among the fastest US app launches on record, with early retention above the average for rival AI apps, and says a large and rising share of Meta's own ad spend now goes to it. That ad spend likely explains much of the install curve, and Meta can run the same ads for any product it owns.  1. Tasks completed. Nothing Meta or Sensor Tower has reported says how many sessions end in a booking, a purchase or a message sent for the user. Those are what a user would pay for, and in our view they are also where a merchant fee could come from.  2. Where the revenue shows up first. In our view Muse's first financial effect is on the ad business Meta already runs. When shopping happens inside Muse, Meta sees the whole path from what a user wants to what they buy, which sharpens its ad targeting. If users start shopping in Muse, Meta can also sell sponsored placement in its answers. Further out, ads could become part of the conversation itself, something we suggested earlier for Meta AI and which applies even more to an agent like Muse. A user preparing for their first marathon with Muse could be offered trainers, energy gels and hydration products in a conversational manner as the plan takes shape, rather than seeing an ad placed beside it. We expect Muse to show up in ad pricing before it appears as a subscription or a take rate.  3. The sharing suspension. Meta paused conversation sharing after security researchers found shared chats could expose personal and business information. That suggests people are already giving Muse real work with real data and sharing it with colleagues. It also means workplace use will meet the data-handling limits that slowed enterprise use of consumer chatbots.  A real catalyst for $META will be Meta disclosing how many tasks and transactions Muse completes, especially if the numbers are impressive.

if you're an ai startup about to do a big launch on x, read this before spending $100,000  :  a head of growth told me their launch videos do 300-500k views and bring in 40 to 100 demo calls.  but he had no idea what happened to everyone else who hit the site, or what to fix to convert more of them  and most launch sites get made the same way. take the first few outputs claude gives you, ship it the night before, disappear into the sameness.  buyers can spot a half-effort launch instantly now.  we've worked with brands doing major launches, and before one goes out i make the founder check five things:  1. position as the leader of a niche, not the product with the most features.  a launch doesn't create positioning, it amplifies whatever you already have. if your launch says "everything the category leader does, plus more", you're paying to remind people the leader exists.  so before we write a word, we audit the whole funnel of everyone they compete with: site, socials, decks, launch posts. when a competitor plays one angle across every touchpoint, that's where they're strongest. fighting them there is expensive and you'll lose.  find the niche nobody owns and claim it outright. a buyer would rather back the best tool for their exact problem than the one with the longest feature list.  2. sell the outcome, not the mechanism.  an enterprise buyer doesn't sign off on how your product works. they sign off on what changes after they buy it: hours saved, cost cut, revenue moved.  so every section should answer "what does this get me?" before "how does it do it?"  and that outcome has to back the niche from point 1. if you're positioning as the tool for finance teams, the ROI on the page should be the number a finance lead gets measured on.  3. coupled your credibility  with "how it works" section  an enterprise buyer evaluates the company before the product. the question they won't say out loud is whether you'll still be around after they've staked their name on you.  i went through a founder's sales calls once. the site had every use case up front, and the first thing buyers still felt was "is this company even legit?" no proof anywhere near the top.  what answers it: real customers they'd recognise, the product actually running instead of a render, a real team behind it, and security and compliance where a finance or security lead will actually find it. all of that has to land before the feature list, not after it.  4. make the brand look the same everywhere a buyer touches you.  a launch sends people to every surface you have at once: the site, the founder's profile, the cold email in their inbox, the deck someone forwards, the docs.  if each one looks like a different person made it, buyers read a company that isn't put together yet. if they all match, you look bigger than you are.  so the email signature, the team's profile pictures, the social banners, the launch video, the deck template and the product UI all have to pull from one system.  greptile is the best example of this i know. the whole brand is one idea: "we find bugs in your codebase" became a green lizard that kills bugs. [NEED: where the lizard shows up, e.g. profile pictures, emails, swag, docs]  you recognise them before you read the logo, in a category where everyone else ships the same abstract gradient.  (we built their 2025 rebrand and design system: 200+ components with dev-first docs, so the team ships it the same way every time.)  5. treat the launch as a perception event and sales funnel  in b2b, a launch rarely sells anything on the day. what it does is set what your market thinks of you.  the video gets you seen. what people decide about you comes from where they click next: your site, the founder's profile, the deck someone forwards.  if the positioning is sharp, they remember you as the company for their exact problem. if the design looks like a company that plans to last, a champion can forward you without having to defend you. if the brand holds up across every touchpoint, you look like you lead the category instead of trying to get into it.  that's authority. and authority is what shows up as pipeline: inbound that already names your niche, champions who bring you in without being sold, open deals that stop stalling on "will they still be around?"  a launch gets you attention for about a day.  whether that day turns into pipeline is decided by the brand they land on.

Most teams scale AI coding agents and end up drowning in unreviewable spaghetti. Lauren Tan ("Potato") spent 6 months engineering the environment around Grokbot so bad code becomes mathematically impossible to merge.  Grokbot + Custom Linters + Chrome DevTools + TLA+ + Lean + Bombadil  Zero markdown prompt bloat. Zero manual line-by-line PR reviews.  She flipped the entire agent trust model upside down—investing from deterministic code at the bottom up instead of begging an LLM to behave inside AGENTS,md:  01 / Categorically ban footguns in the linter LLMs love patching race conditions with `setTimeout` or misusing React's `useEffect`. Her team banned both from product code via strict lint rules whose error messages force the agent to fix the root cause instead of papering over it.  02 / Outlaw 99% of code comments Your repo is the agent's largest input—anti-patterns spread like weeds. Worse, comments go stale and give agents an "escape hatch" to justify hacky workarounds. Delete the comments, force self-documenting types.  03 / Formal & runtime verification over human code review Engineers stopped reading diffs and started reviewing verification artifacts (videos, screenshots, state charts): → Chrome DevTools Protocol & custom CLIs for live runtime inspection → TLA+ for model-checking user flows → Lean for mathematically proving core algorithms like UI virtualization → Bombadil for property-based UI fuzzing  04 / Automate the outer loop On every release, Grokbot spins up cloud agents that fuzz the app like a real user, catch regressions, open fix PRs, and auto-merge them.  Here is the uncomfortable truth nobody writing 500-line prompt files wants to hear:  Roughly 70% of their daily token budget goes strictly to verification—not code generation.   If your inner loop has weak types and no deterministic checks, throwing 10x more agents at your repo just generates slop 10x faster.
